display_name: d'Arenberg The High Trellis Cabernet Sauvignon, McLaren Vale
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "A McLaren Vale Cabernet built from warm coastal sites and named for its training system, The High Trellis delivers ripe black-fruit density and firm tannins at a commonly accessible price point. The 2020 at 14.5% ABV reads as a warm-climate Cabernet with concentrated cassis, black plum, and a backbone of cedar from oak maturation.",
  "wine_summary": "This wine matters because it represents d'Arenberg’s everyday Cabernet from McLaren Vale, a region where Mediterranean warmth meets cooling sea breezes from Gulf St Vincent. d'Arenberg is known in the region for classically styled reds; The High Trellis translates McLaren Vale’s terra rossa, red-brown earth and sand soils into a Cabernet that leans toward ripe dark fruit and structural grip rather than overt green bell pepper or vegetal notes. In bottle you get the regional signature — cassis and black-plum core, firm, grippy tannins from Cabernet’s thick skins, and oak-derived cedar and dark chocolate tones that signal extraction and maturation choices.",
  "terroir_expression": "McLaren Vale’s geology — coastal plains rising toward the Mount Lofty foothills, with terra rossa over limestone in places and pockets of red-brown earth, sand and dark cracking clay — produces Cabernet with ripe fruit concentration and a mineral sapidity when vines access limestone-derived calcium. The coastal influence moderates heat, so while the wine is ripe and high in alcohol, there’s still acidity to lift the dark-fruit flavors and keep tannins from feeling flabby; the clay and red-brown earth help create the wine’s density and firm tannic structure.",
  "vinification_summary": "Detailed public vinification notes for this bottling are limited; typical McLaren Vale Cabernet practice applies: careful extraction during fermentation to balance phenolic ripeness and tannin, followed by aging in oak to integrate tannins and add vanillin/toast notes. Malolactic fermentation (the conversion of sharper malic acid into softer lactic acid) is usually completed in these styles to round acidity and add textural weight, and extended skin contact produces the wine’s deep color and grip.",
  "food_pairing": "1) Char-grilled ribeye with roasted bone marrow — the wine’s firm tannins and high alcohol cut through the ribeye’s fat while cassis and dark-chocolate notes echo the meat’s char. 2) Slow-braised beef cheek ragu over pappardelle — concentrated fruit stands up to the gelatinous texture and long-cooked intensity. 3) Lamb shoulder with rosemary and garlic (roasted low and slow) — herbal rosemary ties to Cabernet’s cedar/tobacco notes and tannin frames the fattier lamb. 4) Aged English cheddar or Comté at 12+ months — savory, slightly crystalline cheeses match the wine’s tannin and bring out dried-plum flavors. 5) Casual: Nashville hot chicken sandwich — spicy heat and fried chicken need the wine’s fruit sweetness and alcohol to carry spice while tannin refreshes the palate.",
  "comparable_wines": "Wynns Coonawarra Estate Cabernet Sauvignon — comparable for its cassis core and firm tannin structure though Coonawarra’s cooler terra rossa often gives more herbal lift. Coriole Cabernet Sauvignon (McLaren Vale) — similar regional ripeness and coastal moderation, offering a useful bench-mark within McLaren Vale for black-fruited, oak-framed Cabernet.",
  "style_profile": "Cabernet Sauvignon — full-bodied with firm tannins and ripe dark-fruit concentration",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through the next 8–12 years; decant for an hour if serving younger to soften primary tannins. Store at ~13–15°C on its side in stable humidity to avoid cork drying.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: US$25–40 retail. Competitors at that level include Wynns Coonawarra Estate Cabernet and everyday offerings from Coriole. The High Trellis is worth the price if you want a ripe, oak-framed McLaren Vale Cabernet with clear varietal character and aging potential; you get density and structure that often exceed other bottles in the same band.",
  "market_position": "This sits on retail shelves as an approachable regional Cabernet for drinkers who want more structure than supermarket blends — commonly listed on wine-focused restaurant lists and available in independent wine retailers. The audience is consumers who appreciate bold Australian reds: young professionals buying by flavor profile and smaller collectors who want drinkable bottles with cellaring upside.",
  "insider_take": "Buy this if you want a warm-climate Cabernet with real tannic backbone rather than a plush, oak-sweet New World style; skip it if you prefer lean, herb-driven Cabernet from Coonawarra. Many shoppers mistake McLaren Vale fruit for fully jammy wines, but The High Trellis keeps enough acidity and oak structure to cellar and pair with savory food.",

parsed.hook: A McLaren Vale Cabernet built from warm coastal sites and named for its training system, The High Trellis delivers ripe black-fruit density and firm tannins at a commonly accessible price point. The 2020 at 14.5% ABV reads as a warm-climate Cabernet with concentrated cassis, black plum, and a backbone of cedar from oak maturation.
parsed.wine_summary: This wine matters because it represents d'Arenberg’s everyday Cabernet from McLaren Vale, a region where Mediterranean warmth meets cooling sea breezes from Gulf St Vincent. d'Arenberg is known in the region for classically styled reds; The High Trellis translates McLaren Vale’s terra rossa, red-brown earth and sand soils into a Cabernet that leans toward ripe dark fruit and structural grip rather than overt green bell pepper or vegetal notes. In bottle you get the regional signature — cassis and black-plum core, firm, grippy tannins from Cabernet’s thick skins, and oak-derived cedar and dark chocolate tones that signal extraction and maturation choices.
parsed.terroir_expression: McLaren Vale’s geology — coastal plains rising toward the Mount Lofty foothills, with terra rossa over limestone in places and pockets of red-brown earth, sand and dark cracking clay — produces Cabernet with ripe fruit concentration and a mineral sapidity when vines access limestone-derived calcium. The coastal influence moderates heat, so while the wine is ripe and high in alcohol, there’s still acidity to lift the dark-fruit flavors and keep tannins from feeling flabby; the clay and red-brown earth help create the wine’s density and firm tannic structure.
parsed.vinification_summary: Detailed public vinification notes for this bottling are limited; typical McLaren Vale Cabernet practice applies: careful extraction during fermentation to balance phenolic ripeness and tannin, followed by aging in oak to integrate tannins and add vanillin/toast notes. Malolactic fermentation (the conversion of sharper malic acid into softer lactic acid) is usually completed in these styles to round acidity and add textural weight, and extended skin contact produces the wine’s deep color and grip.
parsed.food_pairing: 1) Char-grilled ribeye with roasted bone marrow — the wine’s firm tannins and high alcohol cut through the ribeye’s fat while cassis and dark-chocolate notes echo the meat’s char. 2) Slow-braised beef cheek ragu over pappardelle — concentrated fruit stands up to the gelatinous texture and long-cooked intensity. 3) Lamb shoulder with rosemary and garlic (roasted low and slow) — herbal rosemary ties to Cabernet’s cedar/tobacco notes and tannin frames the fattier lamb. 4) Aged English cheddar or Comté at 12+ months — savory, slightly crystalline cheeses match the wine’s tannin and bring out dried-plum flavors. 5) Casual: Nashville hot chicken sandwich — spicy heat and fried chicken need the wine’s fruit sweetness and alcohol to carry spice while tannin refreshes the palate.
parsed.comparable_wines: Wynns Coonawarra Estate Cabernet Sauvignon — comparable for its cassis core and firm tannin structure though Coonawarra’s cooler terra rossa often gives more herbal lift. Coriole Cabernet Sauvignon (McLaren Vale) — similar regional ripeness and coastal moderation, offering a useful bench-mark within McLaren Vale for black-fruited, oak-framed Cabernet.
parsed.style_profile: Cabernet Sauvignon — full-bodied with firm tannins and ripe dark-fruit concentration
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through the next 8–12 years; decant for an hour if serving younger to soften primary tannins. Store at ~13–15°C on its side in stable humidity to avoid cork drying.
parsed.value_assessment: Price: US$25–40 retail. Competitors at that level include Wynns Coonawarra Estate Cabernet and everyday offerings from Coriole. The High Trellis is worth the price if you want a ripe, oak-framed McLaren Vale Cabernet with clear varietal character and aging potential; you get density and structure that often exceed other bottles in the same band.
parsed.market_position: This sits on retail shelves as an approachable regional Cabernet for drinkers who want more structure than supermarket blends — commonly listed on wine-focused restaurant lists and available in independent wine retailers. The audience is consumers who appreciate bold Australian reds: young professionals buying by flavor profile and smaller collectors who want drinkable bottles with cellaring upside.
parsed.insider_take: Buy this if you want a warm-climate Cabernet with real tannic backbone rather than a plush, oak-sweet New World style; skip it if you prefer lean, herb-driven Cabernet from Coonawarra. Many shoppers mistake McLaren Vale fruit for fully jammy wines, but The High Trellis keeps enough acidity and oak structure to cellar and pair with savory food.
